A practical output object could be:

The full classifier stack
1. Encode context   Raw context -> typed ML scores and hyperbolic embedding2. Project into hyperbolic task space   z_x ∈ H^d3. Score class prototypes   distance to Search, Verify, Write, Conflict, LoopRisk, etc.4. Apply grammar constraints   remove illegal transitions5. Compute soft distribution   p(next_state | current_state, x)6. Detect singularity   check ties, boundary escape, loop pressure, contradiction pressure7. Update state machine   choose or sample next legal state

The rest is not decorative, but it is conditional load-bearing.
Hyperbolic geometry becomes load-bearing if you want hierarchy/depth/rabbit-hole detection.
Singularity theory becomes load-bearing if you want robust ambiguity/failure detection.
Group actions become load-bearing if you want symmetry compression.
The full ZZZ becomes load-bearing if you want global probabilistic diagnostics.
But the v0 system does not need the entire tower. It needs the typed scorer, classifier, graph state machine, uncertainty, and state updates.

## User
Think about group actions over graphs as a decimation of autoencoder attention which is every to every element
---
## Assistant
Yes. That is a strong framing.
You can think of group actions over graphs as a principled way to decimate all-to-all attention.
Raw attention says:
every token/state/object can attend to every other token/state/object\text{every token/state/object can attend to every other token/state/object}every token/state/object can attend to every other token/state/object
So for nnn objects, the attention matrix is:
A∈Rn×nA \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times n}A∈Rn×n
That is expensive and mostly unconstrained.
A group action says:
H↷VH \curvearrowright VH↷V
where HHH acts on the graph’s vertices, tasks, memories, tools, or grammar objects. This action identifies objects that are equivalent under some symmetry.
Then instead of attending over every individual pair:
(i,j)(i,j)(i,j)
you attend over orbit pairs:
([i],[j])([i],[j])([i],[j])
where:
[i]={h⋅i:h∈H}[i] = \{h\cdot i : h\in H\}[i]={h⋅i:h∈H}
So the attention matrix is decimated from:
V×VV\times VV×V
to:
(V/H)×(V/H)(V/H)\times(V/H)(V/H)×(V/H)
That is the quotient-attention version.
The core idea
All-to-all attention is a dense relation space.
A group action compresses it by saying:
these objects are the same kind of thing for this computation.
So:
attention over objects→attention over equivalence classes\text{attention over objects}
\to
\text{attention over equivalence classes}attention over objects→attention over equivalence classes
or:
full graph→quotient graph\text{full graph}
\to
\text{quotient graph}full graph→quotient graph
This is exactly a kind of decimation.
In agent terms
Suppose the agent has many evidence sources:
paper_1paper_2paper_3blog_1docs_1github_issue_1
Raw attention compares everything to everything.
But the grammar/group action can identify equivalent roles:
academic_sourcedocumentation_sourcecode_discussion_source
Then the agent attends first to source types:
query -> academic_sourcequery -> documentation_sourcequery -> code_discussion_source
and only later expands inside a type if needed.
So the compression is:
tokens/sources→typed orbits→quotient graph→local refinement\text{tokens/sources}
\to
\text{typed orbits}
\to
\text{quotient graph}
\to
\text{local refinement}tokens/sources→typed orbits→quotient graph→local refinement
That is much more structured than flat attention.
Autoencoder analogy
An autoencoder has:
x→z→x^x \to z \to \hat{x}x→z→x^
where zzz is a compressed latent representation.
Here the quotient graph is the latent bottleneck:
Γ→Γ/H→Γ^\Gamma
\to
\Gamma/H
\to
\widehat{\Gamma}Γ→Γ/H→Γ
where:
Γ\GammaΓ is the full attention/task graph;
HHH is the symmetry/equivalence group;
Γ/H\Gamma/HΓ/H is the compressed graph;
Γ^\widehat{\Gamma}Γ is the reconstructed or refined graph.
So group action gives the encoder a rule:
merge nodes in the same orbit\text{merge nodes in the same orbit}merge nodes in the same orbit
and the decoder a rule:
expand orbit-level decisions back to members\text{expand orbit-level decisions back to members}expand orbit-level decisions back to members
This is not just compression. It is typed compression.

Why this is better than arbitrary pooling
Naive pooling says:
compress because we need fewer nodes.
Group-action decimation says:
compress only along declared equivalences.
That matters because it preserves semantics.
For example, these may be interchangeable:
source_Asource_Bsource_C
But these are not:
sourceclaimcontradictionvalidator
The group action tells the system what can safely be collapsed.
So the quotient graph is not just smaller. It is smaller in a way that preserves invariants.
Relation to attention
Full attention learns:
AijA_{ij}Aij​
for many pairs.
Group-equivariant attention imposes:
Ahi,hj=AijA_{h i, h j} = A_{ij}Ahi,hj​=Aij​
for every group element hhh.
Meaning:
if two pairs are equivalent under the group action, they should share attention behavior.
This reduces degrees of freedom.
Instead of learning every pair independently, the model learns attention by orbit type.
So the number of attention parameters/effective relations drops from roughly:
O(n2)O(n^2)O(n2)
to something closer to:
O(∣(V×V)/H∣)O(|(V\times V)/H|)O(∣(V×V)/H∣)
That is the real decimation.
Where singularities enter
When you quotient by a group action, singularities appear where stabilizers increase.
For a node xxx, its stabilizer is:
Hx={h∈H:h⋅x=x}H_x = \{h\in H : h\cdot x=x\}Hx​={h∈H:h⋅x=x}
Generic nodes have small stabilizers.
Special ambiguous nodes have larger stabilizers.
In attention terms:
a singularity appears where multiple attention targets become indistinguishable under the quotient.
Agent example:
SearchMoreVerifyWrite
If the model cannot distinguish them because their scores become symmetric or tied, the quotient creates a singular decision point.
So quotient attention naturally exposes:
ambiguity;
redundancy;
indistinguishable tools;
equivalent plans;
unstable decision boundaries.
This connects directly to our singularity detector.
Hyperbolic version
If the graph lives in hyperbolic geometry, the group action can decimate attention by hierarchy.
Instead of all-to-all attention across the whole tree, you can attend at levels:
root goal  -> subgoal orbit    -> evidence orbit      -> source orbit        -> token/source detail
So attention becomes multiscale:
global root attention→branch attention→orbit attention→local token attention\text{global root attention}
\to
\text{branch attention}
\to
\text{orbit attention}
\to
\text{local token attention}global root attention→branch attention→orbit attention→local token attention
This is very natural for research agents.
The hyperbolic radius gives specificity.
The angular direction gives semantic branch.
The group action identifies equivalent nodes within a branch or across branches.
The quotient graph gives the compressed state machine.
This gives a concrete architecture
1. Start with dense object graph   tokens, claims, sources, tasks, tools, memories2. Define typed symmetries   equivalent sources, interchangeable tools, repeated subtasks, same grammar role3. Compute orbits   group objects into equivalence classes4. Build quotient graph   nodes are orbits, edges are induced relations5. Run attention/message passing on quotient graph   cheap, structured, typed6. Expand only where needed   if an orbit is high-risk, high-IDF, or singular, refine it back into members
So the agent does not attend to everything always.
It attends like this:
coarse quotient first\text{coarse quotient first}coarse quotient first
refine only high-pressure regions\text{refine only high-pressure regions}refine only high-pressure regions
That is exactly decimated attention.
IDF fits here too
Common orbits can stay compressed:
ordinary sourceordinary search stepordinary summary claim
Rare/high-IDF orbits should be expanded:
contradictionedge-case sourcedecision tieloop singularityunusual transition

Is it overbuilt?
Potentially, yes.
A classical ML person would ask:
Which parts improve prediction/control beyond a concept bottleneck plus finite-state controller?
The load-bearing experiment would be:
Baseline: classifier + finite-state machine.
Add typed grammar.
Add graph structure.
Add distribution/uncertainty.
Add IDF rarity weighting.
Add hyperbolic geometry.
Add singularity detector.
Add group quotienting.
Then measure whether each layer helps.
If hyperbolic geometry, singularity theory, and group quotients do not improve routing, calibration, transfer, or debugging, they are ornamental. If they do improve those things, then the architecture is genuinely stronger.
